full_judgment:
2. Facts in short are, that the petitioner, a fisherman of Co-operative Society, namely Sarping Matshajibi Samabaya Samity applied for taking settlement of the fishery namely, Chatla Beel Group Fishery situated in Baralekha Upazilla of Moulvi Bazar District when the same was eligible for fresh settlement from 1.4 1982 and the Minister of State of the Ministry of Fishery and Livestock passed an order on 15-8-85 for settlement of the said fishery with the petitioner at 50% enhanced rate over the present rate. Pursuant to the said order the District Fishery Development Officer, Sylhet intimated the petitioner that the petitioner have been granted lease of the fishery for the term of 1389 BS to 1394 BS at the annual rent of Taka 1,20,000 vide memo dated 20-8-81 (Annexure B). The said Memo also stipulated the terms and conditions under which the lease was granted. On receipt of the said Memo the petitioner deposited rent for the year 1389 BS on 22-8-81 and the petitioner executed a lease deed signed by the District Fishery Development Officer on behalf of the Government of Bangladesh. It is also the case of the petitioner that the petitioner thereafter submitted a plan for the development of the fishery as per terms of memo dated 20-8-81 and it was approved by the District Fishery Officer. It is the further case that when the petitioner was in possession of the fishery after executing lease deed, Basirpur Fishermen's Co-operative Society Ltd. who was the previous lessee of the said fishery till 1386 BS to 1388 BS colluded with the officers of the respondent No. 1, namely, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms to cancel the lease of the petitioner and it was eventually cancelled on the plea that it was leased out to them before expiry of the previous lease and hence void and the said fishery was settled with the Basirpur Fishermen's Co-operative Society Ltd. By way of extension without any notice to the petitioner. The petitioner thereafter filed a Writ petition being Writ petition No. 19 of 1982 praying for a declaration that the cancellation of the lease of the petitioner and extending the lease of Basirpur Fishermen's Co-operative Society Ltd. was without lawful authority. The Court after hearing the parties vide judgment dated 8-3-82 made the Rule absolute and set-aside the cancellation order. It is the further case of the petitioner that the fishery is a closed fishery and hence steps are to be taken for development of the fishery by putting bamboo Dal, for rearing the fish for two years to fish in the third year and the petitioner, having taken settlement of the fishery for six years, was required to undertake the development work once in every three years and the petitioner in fact undertook and completed the development work for the first term of three years which expired on 13-3-85 i.e. 30th Chaitra 1391 BS and as a matter of fact the District Fishery Development Officer had also issued a certificate to the effect on 4-4-84, that the petitioner had satisfactorily completed the development work of the first term. As to the payment of rent it is the case of the petitioner that he has paid the first lease money amounting to Taka 1,20,000 for 1389 BS when it came to the knowledge of the petitioner that the annual rent of the fishery was only Taka 72,000 and as ordered by the Minister to pay 50 % enhanced rate, rent of the fishery for the term 1389 BS would be Taka 1,08, 000 and hence the petitioner filed a petition before the District Fishery Development Officer on 4-5-1983 asking permission to deposit @ Taka 1,08,000 per year as rent. The District Fishery Development Officer vide his memo dated 10-5-83 allowed the petitioner to pay rent at that rate and ordered to adjust the excess amount paid for 1389 BS against the rent of 1390 BS, pursuant to the said direction the petitioner paid Taka 90,000 for 1390 BS after adjustment of the excess amount of Taka 12,000 paid for the year 1389 BS, by mistake. The petitioner also paid Taka 1,08,000 for the year 1391 BS. It is the further case of the petitioner that the officials of the Government were not very happy with the petitioner because of tie decision given by the Hon'ble Court in Writ Petition No. 19 of 1982 and they have been always trying to defeat the right of the petitioner in respect of the fishery and with that end in view the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar suddenly put the fishery in auction on 25-5-84 for the period 1391 BS to 1393 BS in spite of the petitioner's existing lease. The petitioner objected to the holding of auction and some-how the fishery was omitted from the auction list. 

 5. Respondent No. 3, namely Towhid Fishermen's Co-operative Society Ltd. who according to the respondent No. 1 is in physical possession of the fishery also appeared and contested the Rule by filing a written objection wherein it has been stated that Chatal Beel Group Fishery is situated in Kulaura Upazilla of Moulvi Bazar District and not Baralekha Upazilla and that local officials demanded rent from the petitioner and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) directed the Upazila Nirbahi Officer for making enquiry whether the petitioner undertook any development work and on enquiry it was found that no development work was ever undertaken by the petitioner, so the lease of the petitioner was legally cancelled. It was further stated that the instant certificate from the District Fishery Officer has been managed by the petitioner for the purpose of this writ petition suppressing the report submitted by the Upazilla Nirbahi Officer, Kulaura, to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar to the effect that the petitioner did not take any development work nor paid any rent for 1392 BS and part of 1393 BS and annexed copies of the report of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue). Moulvi Bazar which is marked as Annexure X(i). 

 6. The petitioner filed affidavit-in-reply to the affidavit in opposition filed by the respondent No.1 and respondent No 3 and reiterated what was stated earlier asserting further that the disputed fishery falls within the Baralekha Upazilla and a small part of it falls within Kulaura Upazilla asserting further that under the terms of the settlement the petitioner is to undertake development work under the supervision and guidance of the Directorate of Fishery and the petitioner was never given any direction by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms to take measure for development work under the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) or the Upazilla Nirbahi Officer of Kulaura and there was no question of failure of any terms and condition of settlement. It is further stated that the Upazilla Nirbahi Officer of Baralekha issued notices on 29-4-84 upon the petitioner to produce approved plan and to submit receipt and that the petitioner produces the plan and receipt of payment of rent but the said Officer did not make any enquiry nor did Revenue Officer Kulaura did make any enquiry as to the development work and in fact Upazilla Nirbahi Officer or the Revenue Officer Kulaura had no jurisdiction over the disputed fishery and the petitioner did not receive any notice of any enquiry, enquiry report is a paper work only without any actual enquiry and as per terms of the settlement the District Fishery Development Officer was the competent person to say whether the petitioner undertook the development work and hence it is not correct to say that his certificate is not acceptable, further, stating that the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 did never take over possession of the disputed fishery from the petitioner but he is still in possession of the same. 

 "In annexure A to the Writ Petition which is the impugned order shows that the Pourashava forfeited the aforesaid money in term of the tender notice which is a part of the contract. The question there-fore is one of jurisdiction of the High Court in writ matters. Can the High Court pass an order to refund earnest money or security deposit made as one of the stipulations of the contract? The facts stated earlier and the clause just quoted indicate that the forfeiture of the earnest money on the basis of which the first respondent made a bid and on his failure to pay the bid money, the action of the forfeiture of earnest money was taken. As regards the other action no leave has been granted and we are not called upon to enter into that question. But the question whether forfeiture, made in terms of the contract or not by the Chittagong Pourashava was not a matter justifiable in writ Jurisdiction and so it could not be agitated befores the High Court exercising its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution, commonly known as writ jurisdiction. It is well settled that disputes which arise essentially from contract are not cognisable under writ jurisdiction." 

 Clause (iii) of the lease agreement stated that the lessee shall have to abide by all other terms and conditions as framed or that may be framed by the Government from time to time and any deviation from any of the terms and conditions will make liable for cancellation of the settlement. 

 19. Another reasons which prompted the Government to cancel the lease of the petitioner was that he had not undertaken the development work of the instant fishery as required under the terms of the contract. On an examination of the Memo dated 20-8-81 it is seen that one of the condition of lease was that the petitioner will have to undertake development work of the fishery under the supervision and guidance of the Fishery Directorate. It was provided that the lease document will be executed only on production of development plan. This development work need to be done to the satisfaction of the lessor. In the instant case on a reference to the lease document at clause 8 it appears that the fishery need to be developed under the direction as issued by the fishery department which the lessee would be bound to honour. In sub-clause 'Uma' it was stipulated that if the lessee during the subsistence of the lease period made breach of any of the conditions of the lease or neglects to honour any of the condition of the lease then his lease would be cancelled before termination of the lease and all the lease money will be forfeited to the Government. This lease document was executed in August, 1981 and on the same day the memo was issued containing the terms and conditions of the settlement. It was also issued to the petitioner lessee from the office of the District Fishery Development Officer, Sylhet. It appears that almost one year thereafter in the month of August, 1982 the management of all fishery and livestock was re-allotted to be under the administrative control of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms by the Government. It is seen from paragraph 4 of the petition that the petitioner stated clearly in that paragraph that in 1982 the management was re-transferred under the control of the ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. 

 20. Therefore, it is to the knowledge of the petitioner that from August, 1982 onward the relevant authority in matters of fishery would be the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. But from the Annexure C to the petition it is seen that the lessee on 27-3-84 applied to the Thana Fishery Officer, Baralekha for a certificates as to the satisfactory completion of the development work by him of the Chatla Beel Group Jalmahal and vide Memo dated 23-5-84 the District Fishery Officer Sylhet wrote to the petitioner that from the enquiry report of Upazilla Fishery Officer, Baralekha the development work of first pile period i.e. 1389 BS to 1391 BS of the Chatla Beel Group Fishery under Baralekha Upazilla has been done by him as per plan and he was instructed by the said fishery officer to start development work for the 2nd pile period i.e. 1292 BS to 1394 BS, under proper guidance of Upazilla Fishery Officer, Baralekha. From Annexure C it appears that the Upazilla Fishery Officer, Baralekha by his letter addressed to District Fishery Officer recommended that the Ejaradar may be issued a certificate as to the satisfactory completion of the development work of the instant fishery. From Annexure Y to the affidavit in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent Government it appears that the Upazilla Nirbahi Officer, Kulaura being asked by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Moulvi Bazar on 4-3-85 to report as to the development work of the Chatra Beel Group Fishery. For 1389 BS to 1391 BS reported that he after having enquired into the matter as required by Upazilla Revenue Officer, Kulaura came to know that there is no record of this lease in the office but it transpires on enquiry from the office of the Upazilla Fishery Development Officer, Kulaura that said beel has been leased out by the fishery officer, Sylhet and possession was delivered to the lessee by the office of the Fishery Directorate and that from enquiry of the Upazilla Revenue Officer Kulaura and also from other enquiry it reveals that for the year 1389 BS to 1391 BS there was no development work in the said beel. This report is annexed in the affidavit-in-opposition by the Government, a copy of which is given to the petitioner. In reply to that the petitioner had stated in his affidavit-in-reply in paragraph 11 to the effect that under the terms of the lease development work need be done under the guidance of the Fishery Directorate and they are required to comply with all reasonable direction given by the Fishery Directorate as to the development work and the petitioner accordingly undertook development work as directed by the officers of the Fishery Directorate. 

 23. This brings us to a more recent and a wider chapter of promissory estoppel obliging even persons exercising powers in the affairs of the State to do what he is promise bound to do. 

 If an individual would be bound by his promise then why not an executive authority, performing functions in the affairs of the state. 

 30. In the case of Radhakrishna Agarmal vs The State of Bihar, reported in AIR 1977 (SC) at page 1496 the Supreme Court of India had occasion to examine a similar point. In that case the petitioner was granted lease to collect and exploit Sal Seeds from the forest area but the Conservator of Forest increased the royalty during the continuance of the lease and then cancelled the lease. 

 "Rules of Natural Justice are attached to the performance of certain function regulated by statutes or rules made thereunder involving decisions affecting rights of the parties. When a contract is sought to be terminated by the officers of the State purporting to act under the terms of the agreement between parties such action is not taken in purported exercise of a statutory power. The limitation imposed by rule of natural justice cannot operate upon power which are governed by the terms of an agreement. The only question which normally arises in such cases is whether the action complained of is or is not in consonance with the terms of the agreement." 

 Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned counsel has lastly submitted that in any view of the matter the Government in the instant case in leasing out the fishery and for that matter all fisheries would be working under some statutory provisions. In elaborating this point further he submitted that it has been the law that even if the rights of the parties would ultimately relate to the terms of a concluded contract, the contract, if entered into between the parties in exercise of a statutory power namely, under the provisions of an Act of Parliament or Rules made thereunder then the alleged breach would not be merely contractual but a statutory breach and hence would be agitated under Article 102 of the Constitution and the question of natural justice would be immediately attracted. In substantiating this the learned Counsel has referred to section 76 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and also to the provisions of the Fish Protection Ordinance 1959 and submitted that the right of Government to manage Govt. fishery in referable to those laws and that being so it could not be said that Govt. in managing the fishery acted without the blessings of any law as such under the Estate Manual only and a contract. The learned Counsel in support of this proposition has referred to decision reported in AIR 1973 (SC), at page 265 and AIR 1975 (Madras) at page 81. 

 33. On an examination of these ruling it is seen that the Indian Fisheries Act referred to in those judgments is similar to the provisions as contained in the Fish Protection Ordinance, 1959 as in this country. In the Indian Fisheries Act section 6 provided measures for the protection of fish in all fishery and as to how to fish and only on the basis of a licence granted in this behalf. Sub-section (1) of section 6 provided that State Government may make rules for the purpose mentioned in the section by notification. In exercise of that rule making power and in terms of that power the Indian State Government made Rules called the Tamil Nadu Inland Fisheries (Lease and Licence) Rules 1972. Rule 2 deals with the prohibition of fishing without licence in waters under control of Fishery Department. The said Rule provided that no person shall take any fish from the waters specified in Annexure 1 except under a lease or licence granted by the Government or by such authority as may be authorised in accordance with the conditions specified in the appendix to the Annexure 1 of these rules which may be suitably modified or amended from time to time as required. Examining all these, the Madras High Court in the case under reference came to a finding that in leasing out the fishery the Government functionary exercised a power under the Inland Fisheries Rules 1972 ,made under the said Act and not merely under a contract. 

 34. The learned Attorney-General submitted that fishery in this country is managed by the Government as Government khas property like other khas lands under the instruction as contained in the State Manual. The introductory chapter of the State Manual says that the State Manual deals with the principal policy and with the procedure for the management of the properties owned by the Government as khas or acquired by the Government under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This Manual, according to the learned Attorney General consists of administrative directions having no statutory force. Further section 76 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act only authorises the Government to manage the Government fishery after its acquisition which is thus only a permissive law while the Fish Protection Ordinance, 1959 is prohibitory, prohibiting fishing in government fishery without a licence and though the said Ordinance speaks of a Rule to be framed for the purpose of giving effect to the provision of that Ordinance of 1959 no such Rules had yet been made as in the Madras Case referred to by the petitioner and thus those Ordinances are merely enabling laws without making any Rules for the purpose of giving effect to the provision of the Ordinance, only when a question of acting under statutory authority or Rules would arise. 

 35. There is substance in the contention of the learned Attorney-General and it need be considered in the affirmative and we find that fisheries are being leased out by the Government not under any statute but under the Instruction as contained in the State Manual and they being mere administrative instruction, have no statutory force. Hence, it could not be said that though the rights of the parties are referable to a contract in executing the contract the executive authority in the instant case acted under a statute and thus to be regulated by the statute, any violation of which would be enforced under Article 102 of the Constitution.
